title: A shared compilation stack for distributed-memory parallelism in stencil DSLs
problem: DSL compilers are designed in silos, preventing shared infrastructure and creating uncertainty around DSL longevity and adoption at scale. Finite-difference stencil DSLs like Devito, PSyclone, and Open Earth Compiler maintain separate compilation stacks despite solving similar distributed-memory parallelism challenges.
motivation: Shared compilation infrastructure reduces development and maintenance costs while enabling DSL communities to benefit from collective compiler improvements, similar to how the ML community leverages TensorFlow and PyTorch.
method: The authors took MLIR, a compiler framework, and customized it for high-performance computing by adding abstractions for message passing—the coordination mechanism that lets distributed computers work together when running stencil computations (calculations on grids where each point depends on neighboring points, solved in parallel). They integrated this customized MLIR with three stencil DSLs (Devito, PSyclone, and Open Earth Compiler), enabling all three to generate high-performance code by sharing one compiler infrastructure rather than each building and maintaining separate compilation systems.
key_novelty: By customizing the MLIR compiler framework for high-performance computing and adding message-passing abstractions, multiple stencil DSLs can share one compiler instead of building separate ones.
contributions: HPC-tailored MLIR compiler framework with distributed-memory abstractions for stencil computations
Demonstration of shared compiler components across three distinct stencil DSLs
Framework reducing DSL compiler development costs through unified infrastructure
Proof that high-performance code generation can be unified across heterogeneous DSLs
